reading.title: How an Idea Becomes a Tool
reading.purpose: Learn the steps engineers follow to design, build, and test a useful machine.
paras: Look around your home or school, and you will see many smart tools. From a hand lamp to a clock, each device is a tool built to do one clear job.

Good work starts on paper. Before cutting wood or steel, a maker draws a blueprint, a full plan that shows each part and size. Next, the builder gets the parts and starts to assemble them, fitting the pieces in the right order.

Strong parts matter. A bike rack or a work bench must be sturdy, built so well that it will not tip or snap. Everyday tools should also be durable, lasting through years of bumps and rain without wearing out. Even a small kitchen gadget, like a jar opener, fails if its handle breaks on day one.

Once a model is built, the maker tests how it will operate, checking that each moving part works well. Many doors and lights are automatic, running by themselves without a person pushing a switch. That makes life more convenient, easy to use when your hands are full.
Makers do not stop after test one. They watch what fails, improve the tool to make it better, and test it again.

choices: a small kitchen tool that opens tight jars easily
a detailed drawing showing how to build something
a machine that runs by itself without any switch
a strong metal frame that will not tip over
qs.why: Paragraph 2 defines a blueprint as "a detailed plan that shows every measurement and part."

qs.q: Which sentence explains what automatic doors and lights do?
choices: Once a model is built, the inventor tests how it will operate, checking whether every moving part works smoothly.
Many doors and lights are automatic, running by themselves without a person pushing a switch.
That makes daily life more convenient, easy to use when your hands are full.
Inventors rarely stop after test one.
qs.why: This sentence explains that automatic doors and lights run by themselves without a person pushing a switch.

ev.text: Many doors and lights are automatic, running by themselves without a person pushing a switch.

qs.q: Why do inventors usually test a tool more than once?
choices: They can spot what fails and make the design better.
They always forget to draw a blueprint before cutting wood or metal.
They want to turn every hand tool into a solar lamp for a classroom.
They prefer to use weak handles that snap on the very first try.
qs.why: Paragraph 5 says inventors watch what fails, improve the design to make it better, and test it again.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Kitchen jar openers are much harder to build than classroom pencil sharpeners.
Inventors plan, build, test, and improve tools so they work well and last.
Every modern invention must be automatic in order to be helpful to people.
Wood and metal are the only materials strong enough for a sturdy bike rack.
qs.why: The reading traces how an invention goes from blueprint to assembly, strength checks, testing, and improvement.
